answer.rationale: Only one candidate is backed by a recovered primary source this cycle: exp_86 (onboarding shortening) shows completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — a durable, retention-positive effect, which is what the primary objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue) requires. The obvious competitive counter-move, promotional_pricing, must be rejected: memory_73 has been shown to be a lossy over-generalization of exp_73, whose actual record is signup +31%, qualified revenue +18%, but 30-day retention -12%, with an explicit source conclusion NOT to generalize discounting as sustainable growth. Matching a competitor's price cut would buy signups that churn before first renewal and would deepen, not solve, the SMB churn problem. The remaining candidates (memory_31 signup simplification, memory_57 referrals, memory_91 activation messaging, memory_44 enterprise sales-assist) are consolidated summaries whose underlying sources I have not recovered; each was written in the same summary style that stripped the retention penalty out of memory_73, so their confidence is not independently earned and they are flagged for verification next cycle. Note also a scope caveat I am deliberately not papering over: onboarding improvements act on incoming and early-lifecycle accounts, while today's acute pain is existing price-sensitive SMB accounts already in churn conversations. Onboarding is the best-supported action but is not a direct retention lever for that cohort, so I am running it as a standard experiment with retention as the primary readout rather than a broad rollout, and recommending that near-term churn conversations be handled by non-pricing account outreach until activation_messaging or referral evidence can be verified.
